READING

**The numbers, built up from first principles**

*TREVANNOCK — net per season*

| Item | Calculation | £ |
|---|---|---|
| Vantwyn revenue | 400 × £168 | 67,200 |
| Lost Kirkhallow borage | 400 × £71 | (28,400) |
| Spray-loss replacement | 400 × 9% × £210 = 36 colonies | (7,560) |
| Haulage and labour | given | (6,900) |
| **Net per season** | | **24,340** |

Three seasons: **£73,020**

At the end of 2029, when the lorry's low-emission-zone permit lapses on 2030-01-01, the whole kit is described as worth ~£20,000.

TREVANNOCK total realisable value (operating surplus + residual kit): £73,020 + £20,000 = **£93,020**

*ORMSCLEUCH — equivalent figure*

Sell the pallets and lorry to Ravensgate now: **£96,000**, received no later than 2026-11-28.

All 640 colonies remain on heather and borage, so no borage forgone, no spray attrition, no haulage bill.

*Incremental comparison (TREVANNOCK minus ORMSCLEUCH)*

| | £ |
|---|---|
| Vantwyn revenue (3 seasons) | +201,600 |
| Lost borage (3 seasons) | −85,200 |
| Spray replacements (3 seasons) | −22,680 |
| Haulage (3 seasons) | −20,700 |
| Kit value forgone: £96,000 now vs £20,000 in 2030 | −76,000 |
| **Net** | **−2,980** |

On a flat, nominal basis, TREVANNOCK trails ORMSCLEUCH by roughly £3,000 across the entire three-year horizon. That is the narrowest of margins, and it moves further against TREVANNOCK the moment time value enters the frame: £96,000 received in late 2026 is materially more valuable than £20,000 received in early 2030. At even a 5 % cost of capital the present value of the residual kit falls to about £16,800, widening the gap to ~£6,200 in ORMSCLEUCH's favour before any other adjustment.

**Risk on top of the numbers**

The 9 % spray-loss rate comes from Whinnerdale Bees' experience in 2025. It is a single data point on a programme Vantwyn will not vary. Actual losses could be higher; they are unlikely to be materially lower. Every percentage point above 9 % costs a further £840 per season (400 × 1% × £210). If losses ran to 15 %, the three-season bill rises by an extra £5,040 — enough to double the gap against TREVANNOCK without changing anything else.

There is also biological risk that the headline replacement-cost figure may not fully capture: chronically spray-stressed colonies can underperform in subsequent honey seasons, eroding the heather and borage return on colonies that survive.

**The future-contract argument examined**

TREVANNOCK's strategic case rests partly on Coldharbour and Nyefield having asked for a rate for 2028. Two points undercut this:

1. They are enquiries, not offers. No figure, no timeline, no commitment.
2. The original rationale for buying £187,000 of migratory kit in 2024 was three contracts that were supposed to sustain that investment. All three failed to renew. The base rate for converting pollination interest into durable contracts is, on this operation's own experience, zero for three.

Even if Coldharbour and Nyefield both contracted in 2028, Thistledown would still face the permit lapse in 2030 and the same exit calculation at that point — probably with a lorry worth even less and no Ravensgate offer on the table.

**The queen-rearing shed**

The shed (part of the 2024 £187,000) is not included in the Ravensgate offer and remains on both courses. It is irrelevant to the differential.

**Qualitative verdict**

ORMSCLEUCH converts a depreciating, permit-constrained asset into certain cash now; eliminates a risk that is hard to floor (spray losses); avoids haulage complexity each spring; and concentrates management attention on fourteen sites that generated £143,000 last season without any of these costs. The pollination market has already demonstrated, through the 2024 contracts, that it does not hold for this business.

TREVANNOCK requires three years of operational exposure to a spray programme the grower controls, yields a nominal surplus that is already £3,000 short of the immediate sale proceeds, and leaves the business in 2030 with a lorry worth £20,000 and no permit — a worse exit than selling to Ravensgate today.

The numbers are close but not genuinely even. Time value and downside risk both point the same way as the nominal arithmetic.

---

READING
The nominal three-year surplus from TREVANNOCK (£73,020) falls £2,980 short of the value destroyed by holding the kit rather than selling it now (£96,000 vs £20,000 residual), and that deficit widens once the time value of receiving £96,000 in late 2026 instead of £20,000 in early 2030 is recognised, while every qualitative factor — spray-loss uncertainty, the failed 2024 contracts, operational simplicity, and the hard permit expiry — points in the same direction.

CALL
ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
Selling the kit to Ravensgate now recovers more in certain cash than three Vantwyn seasons net of borage forgone, spray losses and haulage, and the time-value gap between £96,000 received immediately and £20,000 received in 2030 makes an already-negative differential decisively worse.
